summary: A giant of the icy Southern Ocean, the colossal squid is the heaviest known invertebrate, armed with rotating hooks on its tentacles and the largest eyes ever studied. For a century it was known almost only from whale stomachs and fishing catches, until a baby was filmed alive in 2025.

stats.size: Estimated up to about 7 m long and 500 kg
stats.depth: Adults about 1,000 m or deeper; juveniles shallower
stats.range: Antarctic waters, reaching north to southern New Zealand

facts.title: Heavyweight champion
facts.text: A colossal squid caught in the Ross Sea in 2007 weighed about 470–495 kg, and scientists estimate the species reaches about 500 kg, making it the heaviest invertebrate known.

facts.title: Hooks that turn
facts.text: The club-shaped tips of its two tentacles carry rotating hooks, and its arms bear hooks too. No other glass squid has them.

facts.title: Record-breaking eyes
facts.text: It has the largest animal eyes ever studied, possibly the largest of any animal in history, useful for spotting faint light in the deep.

facts.title: First seen alive in 2025
facts.text: In March 2025 a remotely operated vehicle filmed a see-through, 30 cm juvenile at 600 m near the South Sandwich Islands: the first confirmed footage of a live colossal squid in its habitat.

facts.title: Whale food
facts.text: Beaks pile up in sperm whale stomachs because they resist digestion. From these, scientists estimate colossal squid could make up a large share of some sperm whales' diet in the Southern Ocean.
